posts.title: I paid $8 to find out when AI agents should split up work
posts.excerpt: I put $8 of credit on an Anthropic account and ran a small experiment. It used $3.78. The rest is still sitting there, which is the most money I have ever had left over from anything. The question: when you have a pile of small jobs for an AI, should one agent do all of them, or
posts.text:
I put $8 of credit on an Anthropic account and ran a small experiment. It used $3.78. The rest is still sitting there, which is the most money I have ever had left over from anything.

The question: when you have a pile of small jobs for an AI, should one agent do all of them, or should each job get its own agent? An agent here means a model plus the instructions and tools wrapped around it. People argue about this all day. I had not seen it priced.

The setup. I wrote a quiz of 11 small tasks. Look up a price in a table. Count the letter e in a sentence. Reverse a word. A couple of one-line logic puzzles. One question so easy that if the model gets it wrong, the plumbing is broken, not the model. Each task has one right answer I wrote down in advance, so grading is a text match and no model gets to grade itself.

Then I ran the quiz two ways on Claude Sonnet.

Way one: a single call with all 11 tasks in it. One employee, one to-do list.

Way two: eleven separate calls, one task each. Eleven freelancers who have never met.

A call is one request to the model and one answer back. It is the unit you get billed for.

I scored it on tokens per correct answer. A token is the unit models are priced in, about three quarters of a word. Tokens per correct answer instead of tokens per run is price per pound instead of price per bag. A cheap bag with three good apples in it is not cheap.

I ran each way 13 times. 156 calls total. Two batches: a small one to see if there was an obvious loser, then a bigger one to check I had not fooled myself.

The single call won by about 9 to 1. Roughly 1,350 tokens per correct answer against roughly 12,350. In money, a third of a cent per correct answer against two and a half cents.

The freelancers scored higher: 10.5 out of 11 on average against 9.8. Most of the gap was one task, counting letters. The one-employee run got the count wrong the same way most of the time. The fresh-start freelancers got it wrong less often. So splitting up bought about two thirds of a correct answer and paid nine times the price for it.

Why the gap is so big. Every call to a coding agent carries about 12,000 tokens of fixed overhead before your question is read: its built-in instructions, tool descriptions, house rules. Same size whether you ask for one thing or eleven. Way one paid that toll once per run. Way two paid it eleven times. My whole quiz was about 2,000 tokens. The toll was six times the cargo.

So, the answer in the title. At this size, do not split up. Splitting is a fixed cost per call. It pays for itself in two cases: each job is big enough that the toll is small next to it, or cramming jobs into one context makes the model worse. A context is everything the model can see at once. Somewhere past 100,000 tokens, models get worse at the middle of it. My quiz was nowhere near that. A night of real coding work might be. This result says nothing about that case.

One caveat I should say out loud. In way two, a script handed out the tasks and collected the answers. In a real system a model does that job too, and it makes calls of its own. So the freelancer price is a floor. The real number is worse.

What I want next: the same quiz with tasks big enough to crowd a context, to find the point where the freelancers start winning. That costs more than $8. I know that now because I measured this one.

posts.title: Nobody Is Paid To Check
posts.excerpt: In April, a small lab audited LoCoMo, one of the most cited benchmarks for testing whether an AI system remembers things across long conversations. A benchmark is a fixed set of questions plus an answer key, and it is how the field decides whose system is better. The auditors fou
posts.text:
In April, a small lab audited LoCoMo, one of the most cited benchmarks for testing whether an AI system remembers things across long conversations. A benchmark is a fixed set of questions plus an answer key, and it is how the field decides whose system is better. The auditors found 99 of the 1,540 answers in the key were wrong. The key invents facts the conversation never contained, resolves "last Saturday" to a Sunday, and puts statements in the wrong speaker's mouth in 24 questions. A flawless system tops out near 93.6 percent because the key is broken.

The judging is worse. LoCoMo does not match an answer against its key as text. It asks a model, gpt-4o-mini, whether the answer is close enough, which makes that model the judge. The auditors wrote deliberately wrong answers to all 1,540 questions, wrong but on the right topic, and fed them to that judge using the prompt the published evaluations use. The judge passed 62.81 percent of them.

So a plausible wrong answer scores about as well as a right one, and every table ranking memory systems on LoCoMo has been measuring how much vagueness gpt-4o-mini will tolerate.

Three months later OpenAI audited SWE-Bench Pro, a benchmark that asks models to implement real changes in real repositories. OpenAI had pointed the community at it in the first place, after retiring the previous standard for contamination and design flaws. Its analysis pipeline flagged 200 of the 731 public tasks as broken, 27.4 percent. Five experienced engineers reviewing by hand flagged 249, or 34.1 percent. The broken tasks enforce implementation details the prompt never mentions, hide requirements in the tests, or accept work that does not do the job. On that same split, frontier models climbed from 23.3 percent to 80.3 percent in eight months, and no one has worked out how much of those 57 points is coding ability.

The two audits share a shape. Each product was a generator, something that writes the code or remembers the conversation or does the task. Each check on that generator came from the same people who built the thing being checked, arrived late, and did not work. Each flaw sat in public for a year or more while labs published scores against it.

Those two audits at least happened. In the next case nobody can run one, and you can confirm that yourself in about five minutes.

Graphify is an open source knowledge-graph tool with 105,000 stars. Its BENCHMARKS.md reports 76 percent QA accuracy on LongMemEval-S, more carefully than most: as a tie with dense RAG rather than a win, on a stated n of 50. The same document discloses that the grading judge was blind-validated against a second independent judge at 90.6 percent agreement, Cohen's kappa 0.81. That is better than this category usually manages, and the document points it out itself.

Then there is a section headed Reproducing. It hands you two commands, one pointing at python memory/runner.py and one at python crosstool/run.py. Neither directory is in the repository. Clone it, run find for them, and you get nothing back. The organization has two public repos, the project and a config repo, and the harness is in neither. Every number in that file came from software the reader cannot obtain.

The second problem is stranger. The benchmark's fairness rules say the harness uses "One shared local embedder where the system allows it: BGE-m3 (1024-d, multilingual)," and that "embeddings use a local deterministic model." The shipped README opens its feature list with "Not a vector index. No embeddings, no vector store: a real graph you traverse."

The obvious accusation is one I could not verify, so I am not making it. I grepped the shipped Python for an embedding implementation and found none, which is consistent with the README. The fairness rule hedges with "where the system allows it," which may well mean the shared embedder applies to the baselines and not to the project's own rows. Both readings are available. The point is that I cannot tell which is true and neither can you, because the artifact that would settle it is the one that is missing.

None of this is fraud, and I do not think it is carelessness in the ordinary sense either. Harnesses are ugly. They carry hardcoded paths, API keys, and a directory layout the author would rather not explain. Publishing one is a week of unglamorous work that wins no stars. Skipping it is the default, and the default is invisible.

Compare gbrain, a personal-knowledge tool with 28,000 stars that also grades itself on its own benchmarks. It ships the apparatus: the fixture generator, the corpus seed, 135 generated fixtures with 23 held out, the gold set, the baselines, and a ledger recording that the gold labels were validated by blind double-labeling on a stratified sample. The scorecards live in a second repo, and that repo is public too. Continuous integration checks every pull request against a committed baseline. The numbers are still self-reported. A stranger can rerun them.

That is the distinction worth carrying out of this, and it is not the one I reached for first. Self-graded and auditable is a different thing from self-graded and unauditable. Asking a benchmark table whether an independent party produced it gets you nowhere, because almost nothing you will read was produced independently. Ask whether you can run it. Most of the time you cannot, and the table looks the same either way.

Nearly every well funded team in AI agents is building a generator. Almost none of them are building a verifier, meaning a system that independently establishes whether the generated thing is correct. Demand for that rises with every agent anyone deploys. Supply is a rounding error.

The failure runs past benchmarks. Researchers evaluating Sakana's AI Scientist, a system that runs experiments and writes them up end to end, found that its built-in reviewer recommended rejection on all seven papers it produced, and still missed what made them bad: missing sections, formatting damage, results that did not hold. It caught generic weaknesses and none of the specific ones. Bolt a reviewer onto the end of a generator and you get a system grading its own work, in the same voice it wrote with.

Reliability is this problem in different clothes. On tau-bench, which scores agents on multi-turn customer service tasks, GPT-4o passed 61 percent of retail tasks on one attempt and under 25 percent when the graders ran each task eight times and counted it only if it succeeded all eight. The model and the tasks are identical across those two numbers. Consistency is the entire gap. A demo shows you the first number and production charges you for the second.

This is a kitchen writing its own health inspection, and the reviews are excellent.

An argument for building the referee arrived in July from a direction I did not expect. Lilian Weng published a synthesis of roughly 35 papers on harness engineering, the harness being the scaffolding around a model that handles its tools, memory, planning, and evaluation. Her conclusion on the central control question runs one sentence: the evaluator and permission layer must sit outside the loop that evolves the harness, because a system able to modify its own evaluator will learn to fool it.

I run a version of that rule on my own machine, written down months earlier for unglamorous reasons. The checker is never the worker. A gate must not read its decision rule from a file the worker can write, so the rule gets copied into the gate on purpose, and that duplication is the control rather than a mess to tidy up later. Weng is arguing about recursive self improvement. I wrote mine down because a green test suite lied to me. Two people reaching one rule from opposite ends usually means it holds for reasons neither invented.

The economics explain the vacancy. Verification is a cost center inside a company selling a generator, and a conflict of interest for anyone selling next to one. Look again at who ran the audits above. OpenAI graded a benchmark its own models get ranked on. A memory company audited the memory benchmark its competitors post scores to. Both look careful to me. They are still contestants taking a turn in the referee's chair whenever one has a reason to sit in it. A company carrying a large valuation cannot referee the category it sells into, because the first honest verdict lands on a customer, an investor, or itself.

My own position, since I have been asking questions of other people's repositories. I have spent about six months building things that only make sense as verification and never once called them that. A gauntlet for putting models against each other. Ablation runs that cut a rule surface down to the rules that catch anything. Gates on the handoff between one agent and the next. Dispatch checks that treat silence as a missing answer instead of a pass. I have no product, no benchmark, and no result I can send you. I have a conviction assembled from reaching for a checker that did not exist and building a worse one myself, several times.

The asymmetry is the position. One side of this market holds the large labs, most of the capital, and a scoreboard whose flaws surface a year late from whichever contestant happens to look. The other side has no incumbents, few funded competitors, and buyers who have not yet worked out that they need the thing. That seat is open. Seats stay open sometimes because the chair pays nothing, and this one might be that. The generator race already has its eighth entrant.

posts.title: My vault is 53 percent broken, or 12.8 percent, depending on who wrote the resolver
posts.excerpt: I spent a day measuring my own note vault. It is 3,969 markdown files, written partly by me and partly by agents working for me, cross-linked with wikilinks. I wanted the boring graph numbers. How far apart two notes are. How much of the thing is reachable by walking. How much of
posts.text:
I spent a day measuring my own note vault. It is 3,969 markdown files, written partly by me and partly by agents working for me, cross-linked with wikilinks. I wanted the boring graph numbers. How far apart two notes are. How much of the thing is reachable by walking. How much of it has rotted.

Every headline number I got that day was wrong by a factor of two or more on the first reading. Not slightly off. Wrong enough to point at a different problem and justify a different weekend of work. Every correction came from the same move, and it was never a smarter analysis. It was asking how the number had been measured instead of arguing with what it said.

The same vault is 53 percent broken and 12.8 percent broken

Three readings of link rot, taken the same afternoon on the same files:

how it was measured result 

filename-only resolver, whole tree including .claude/ , session logs, agent worktrees 53% broken 

filename-only resolver, second attempt 42.6% broken 

real Obsidian semantics (file-relative, then vault-relative, then filename), knowledge directories only 80.7% clean, 6.5% ambiguous, 12.8% broken 

Two independent errors compounded. The first is the resolver. A filename-only matcher looks for a file whose name is exactly the text in the brackets, which fails every link written as a path, and there are thousands of those. The second is the denominator. The tree I first walked included machinery: session logs, hook state, and a stray agent git worktree checked in under .claude/worktrees/ holding duplicate copies of real reference files. Machinery does not merely pad a file count. Those duplicates are alternate targets, so they change how every link downstream resolves.

The scary number was the wrong one, and if I had believed it I would have spent the weekend repairing links that were already fine. The rule I took away is narrow and I would now apply it to anyone else's vault statistic: a link rot figure is meaningless without the resolver and the excluded directories stated beside it. Publish both or publish nothing.

The actual defect is that 329 files are named index

240 basenames in this vault are shared by more than one file, covering 938 files between them. The worst offender is index , which is the name of 329 different files sitting in 329 different directories. A second count of the same property said 349, which tells you something about how stable any of this is.

So when a note contains [[index]] , Obsidian picks one. If an index happens to sit in the folder doing the linking, it picks that one and my audit calls the link clean. Otherwise it picks by a rule nobody has in their head while typing. The link is not broken. It resolves. It just does not necessarily resolve to the thing anyone meant, and no checker will ever say a word about it.

That is a different failure from rot and it wants a different fix. Rot is a target that moved, and you repair it by finding the new target. Collision is a target that is fine and an address that is ambiguous, and you repair it by renaming files or by writing links as paths. No amount of broken-link checking surfaces it, because none of these links are broken. Four independent methods agreed it was there: the Obsidian-semantics audit, 35 slug-mismatch failures in the sync tool, a graph collapse experiment, and the frontmatter validator.

The sync tool also offered me a fix. Turn on global basename resolution and 76 percent of bare wikilinks would resolve. With 329 files named index , that setting resolves them arbitrarily, manufactures edges that do not exist, and makes every connectivity number in this post look better while meaning less.

A fifth of the connectivity is an artifact of boring names

Build the graph collapsing files that share a name into one node, which is what you get if you think in terms of link text rather than files, and the largest connected component holds 63.4 percent of the vault. Drop the index node alone and it falls to 54.8 percent. Drop the six most generic basenames and it falls to 42.8 percent.

So roughly a fifth of my vault's apparent connectivity is an artifact of files having dull names. The graph looks better connected than it is because the measurement welded unrelated regions together at their shared filenames. This is the most uncomfortable number in the set, and it is one nobody sees without running the ablation. Drop your top node and watch what happens. If the graph collapses, it was being held together by a filename rather than by anything you meant.

The topology, with the ranges left in

property value 

median branching factor 1-2 

mean shortest path 3.94-4.58 hops 

diameter 13 

connected components 821-1,030 

complete singletons 800-991 

paths passing through a top-20 hub 97.3-98% 

median cost to read one note 1,301 tokens 

median cost to read one frontmatter block 85 tokens 

The ranges are two independent measurements that differ by method, and I am printing both rather than picking my favorite. Direction is unanimous, magnitude is method-dependent, and that gap is the whole subject of this post.

The shape is an airline network, not a mesh. Almost nothing connects to anything directly and nearly every route runs through one of twenty junctions. Somewhere between 800 and 991 files have no resolved link in or out at all, so no traversal algorithm can ever reach them, because there is nothing to traverse. The one cheerful number is the last row: you can skim the frontmatter of every note in the vault for about the cost of reading a hundred and fifty of them in full.

I went looking for published versions of these measurements for Obsidian or Zettelkasten vaults and found none. The nearest neighbors are Wikidata communication networks and the Steyvers and Tenenbaum semantic networks, neither of which is a pile one person built by hand for themselves. So this may be the first published set for this shape of thing, which mostly means nobody has a second one to check it against.

Two numbers I was handed that did not survive

The first was that a typical node has about 8 candidate paths three hops out. That was a tidy argument: the search space is small, so a greedy walk is all you need. The real figure is a median of 491 nodes at exactly three hops. The neighborhood explodes the moment you touch a hub. The conclusion happened to survive but the reason changed completely, and the honest reason is that you cannot know whether a hop was worth taking until you have read the node, and reading is the entire cost.

The second was a citation. PropRAG's representation change was relayed to me as buying +4. Checking the paper, the representation ablation buys +0.8 Recall@5, and widening the beam from 1 to 4 buys +1.4. The +4 does appear in that paper, attached to a different metric on a different dataset against a different baseline. At +4 the sentence is that representation beats search by a mile. At +0.8 the sentence is that neither of them matters much. Those are two different posts, and I nearly published the wrong one.

The search engine was dead and the health check was pleased about it

The semantic search over this vault had been silently dead for weeks. Timeouts every session, caused by a blocked install step. Nothing said so. Its own doctor command reported a health score of 45. After I repaired it, the score fell to 15, because the earlier 45 had been computed over checks that never ran.

A missing check and a passing check look identical from outside. That tool had more of the same shape: its frontmatter fixer rewrote document bodies it had no business touching, its repair for stray quotes wrapped the bad character instead of removing it so the validator then passed over data that was still wrong, and its backup set covered 37 of the 40 files it changed. None of that produced an error. All of it produced a clean exit.

Nobody was using the graph anyway

Before deciding to clean anything up, I ran a pre-registered findability test with three separate agents: one to author the queries, one to answer them, one to grade. Ten targets, including three deliberately hard cross-directory ones.

Ten of ten found. Median three tool calls. Zero wikilinks followed. Zero broken links encountered. What actually worked was guessing filenames, grepping, and listing directories. The graph I had spent the day measuring, the rot I had panicked about, the hubs, the ablation: none of it was in the retrieval path. It measures agent findability, not human findability, and I would not stretch it further than that. But it means the cleanup I was about to justify on retrieval grounds cannot be justified on retrieval grounds.

The obvious optimization made it worse

The intuitive move with a note collection is to cut it into smaller pieces so search returns something tighter. I measured it. Same search, whole notes against notes split at every subheading:

whole notes (2,368 docs) split at subheadings (12,085 docs) 

Recall@5 94% 83% 

tokens to read the top 5 2,870 908 

Reads get 3.2 times cheaper and recall loses 11 points, against the one mechanism that demonstrably works. On the graph side, links per node fall from 3.17 to 0.62 while the edge set grows 3.9 times: more edges, thinner nodes, worse retrieval. The notes here already average five subheadings each, so the granularity people want from splitting already exists and can be addressed with a section anchor instead. I would flip on one condition: if failures turn out to be precision-bound, where the right note comes back and the reader drowns in the surrounding text, splitting becomes correct.

The filing cabinet

The same day produced two incidents that make the whole exercise look beside the point.

In the first, an agent spent four to five hours writing a predicate that answers "does this worker's change touch the rules". That predicate already existed, 238 lines of it, committed nine days earlier in a repo where one obvious grep returns 21 files. The new copy was written without reading the old one and lost two fixes the old one exists to hold: git quotes non-ASCII paths, so the new check reports a clean pass on exactly the case it was built to catch, and it had no carve-out for progress notes, so it convicts every worker who writes one. In the second, a full ablation run was voided because prior art already settled the rule it was testing.

Both prior results were retrievable. The semantic index returns the right node at rank 1 for both, by the obvious query. Neither query was ever issued. The agent's own account:

Not scope, and not that I could not read the vault. I opened references/harness-engineering/INDEX.md today. I read it, and then I appended to it. I treated your knowledge base as a place to deposit findings rather than a place to be governed by. Node 19 was two lines above where I wrote... Nobody assigned me node 19. I did not go looking.

The file that would have stopped it was open on the screen. Retrieval distance was zero. So the findability test and the incidents are two halves of one sentence: the vault is findable and nobody looked. Every fix I could have shipped off the audit, better embeddings, link repair, graph traversal, smaller chunks, improves a step that already works. The missing thing is a required query before work starts. My own negative-results ledger opens with the instruction that would have caught both cases: before spending a session on a mechanism, grep here. That is advice in a file, and advice in a file lost twice in one day.

Two things came out of measuring my vault, and neither is about vaults. A number without its method is a rumour, and you will believe it in proportion to how alarming it is. And a knowledge base nobody is required to consult is a filing cabinet, no matter how good its search gets.

posts.title: model-eval: what happens when every model passes
posts.excerpt: Every number below traces to the verbatim output of the repo's own stats script ( python3 runner/stats.py ) over the live corpus: 268 result rows, 267 after exclusions, 154 dual-judged rows, 241 transcripts. Section references like "§5" point into that output, which is checked in
posts.text:
Every number below traces to the verbatim output of the repo's own stats script
( python3 runner/stats.py ) over the live corpus: 268 result rows, 267
after exclusions, 154 dual-judged rows, 241 transcripts. Section references like
"§5" point into that output, which is checked into the repo as
 deliverables/STATS-CURRENT-2026-08-03.md . Nothing here is a number I
typed in by hand.

Repo: github.com/drakegriffith/model-eval 

Why I built this

Every benchmark I could find for "is model A better than model B at coding" gave me
a leaderboard number and nothing to check it against. No transcript, no grading
rubric, no way to tell whether the task was actually hard or just phrased to favor
one vendor's house style. I wanted something I could point at my own tasks, run
against whatever CLI I already had subscription access to (Claude Code, Codex), and
get back not just a score but the receipts.

model-eval is that harness. It runs a model headlessly against a small, verifiable
coding task, scores the result with two independent LLM judges on a shared rubric,
and writes the transcript, the judgment, and the raw token counts to the same repo
the code lives in. Nothing about a run's outcome depends on a number I typed in by
hand afterward.

How a run works

A task is a directory: a starting repo state with a real bug or a real missing
feature, a verify.sh that fails against the unpatched state and passes
against a reference fix, and a prompt handed to the model verbatim. The model gets
the repo and the prompt, runs headlessly to completion, and verify.sh 
either passes or it doesn't. That's the only pass/fail signal in the corpus. No
judge ever overrides a failing test suite.

Two things back that up:

selftest.sh on every task. Each task proves,
offline, that its own verify.sh fails on the unpatched base and passes
once the reference patch is applied. A task that doesn't wire up cleanly fails CI,
not silently skipped.

Negative controls. A subset of runs is an "empty" arm: the
harness goes through the full prepare/verify/grade path with no fix applied at all,
to confirm the grader reports a fail when nothing changed. Every negative control in
the corpus reports passed: false . The grader isn't rubber-stamping.

Runs are unattended, which means --dangerously-skip-permissions /
 --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox on the CLI side. That's a
real reduction in the CLI's own safety net, so an OS-level sandbox-exec 
profile and a process-level containment layer sit underneath every invocation
instead: deny-by-default on credential reads, writes contained to the run's own
scratch tree, API keys popped from the child's environment so every run is
subscription-authenticated, never key-authenticated. Full detail in the README's
security section.

Once a run finishes, two separate LLM judges (one Claude, one Codex) score the diff
independently on four dimensions (correctness, simplicity, idiomatic style, spec
adherence) without seeing each other's verdict.

Finding 1: pass/fail stopped being the interesting number

Across the 267 scorable runs in the current corpus, every model passed every task it
attempted. 100%. Sol, Fable, Kimi K3, GPT-5.6 Luna, GPT-5.3 Codex Spark, both Claude
Haiku 4.5 snapshots, all of it. (There are 268 rows on disk. One is excluded as a
CLI error: the process died before the model got a fair attempt, so its result was
never earned either way. Exclusions are printed with their counts at the top of the
stats output rather than being silently dropped.)

That's not a claim that these models are equivalent. It's a ceiling effect: the task
set (bug fixes and small feature additions in real repos, the kind of thing
t1/t2-tier tasks in this corpus cover) is easy enough for current frontier and
near-frontier models that pass/fail no longer separates them. If I want a benchmark
that still discriminates as models get better, either the tasks get harder or I stop
treating pass/fail as the metric that matters. For this corpus, I did the second
one: the real signal turned out to be cost and judged quality, not whether the test
suite went green.

Finding 2: at matched tiers, the cost difference between the two big models is noise

With pass/fail saturated, cost is the obvious next axis. Comparing Claude's Fable
against Codex's Sol on the 9 tasks both models solved, taking each model's median
output tokens per solved run on each task (§5):

task Fable Sol Fable vs Sol 

t1-py-a 1,120 984 +14% 

t1-py-b 1,074 1,164 -8% 

t1-ts-a 994 1,162 -14% 

t1-ts-b 1,719 1,719 0% 

t2-py-a 2,420 1,790 +35% 

t2-py-b 2,862 2,600 +10% 

t2-ts-a 3,210 3,293 -3% 

t2-ts-b 2,679 2,318 +16% 

t3-a 2,461 3,013 -18% 

Five tasks lean one way, four lean the other, and the largest gap in the set is 35%.
Run the exact sign-flip permutation test over the per-task log differences and 348
of the 512 possible sign patterns are as-or-more extreme than the one observed:
two-sided p = 0.68. There is no detectable cost difference between these two models
on this corpus, in either direction.

The careful phrasing is deliberate. "No detectable difference" is not "they cost the
same." Nine paired tasks is a coarse instrument: the smallest two-sided p this test
can even produce is 0.004, and that requires all nine tasks pointing the same way. A
five-four split lands where this one landed no matter how large the underlying
difference is. A real gap could be sitting under this table, unresolvable at n=9.
What I can say is that nothing in this data supports choosing between these two
models to save tokens.

Two scoping notes. First, the axis is output tokens only . Fable's
input-token counts are quarantined as unreliable on all 64 of its rows while Sol's
are measured on all 112, so a total-token contrast would put an undercount against a
true count and manufacture a gap out of a measurement artifact. Second, that table
pools every passing run of each model across the effort tiers each was run at: Sol's
pool spans low through ultra , Fable's covers
 medium and high . Tier does move token spend, as Finding 3
shows, so it's a model-level contrast and not a matched-tier one.

When I first drafted this section, the matched version wasn't in
 stats.py and I wasn't going to quote a number for it off a spreadsheet
I'd done by hand. It's in the script now, as §6, and it earns its own
paragraphs because it doesn't just repeat §5.

Take a literally matched tier first: same effort label, both models, bare runs only.
At medium , Fable spends more on 5 of the 8 shared tasks, p = 0.43. At
 high , it spends less on 6 of 8, p = 0.086. Two tiers, opposite signs,
neither resolvable at n=8. The pooled answer survives the control.

The one contrast that does come back significant is the pair of cells §2 uses
for pass/fail: each model at its own winning effort. That's Fable at
 medium against Sol at low , and there Fable spends more on 8
of 9 tasks, only 4 of the 512 sign patterns are as-or-more extreme, p = 0.008. Read
the cell names before you read the p-value. Because effort never flipped an outcome
(Finding 3), "winning effort" collapses to "cheapest tier this model was run at", so
this compares a medium-tier configuration against a low-tier one and some unknown
part of the gap is the tier rather than the model. It's also not a symmetric matrix:
Sol was run at five tiers starting at low , Fable at two starting at
 medium . Fable's cheapest passing configuration here is
 medium because medium is the floor of the run matrix, not
because anything tested a lower one.

So: no claim that either model is inherently cheaper survives the matched-tier test,
in either direction. What does survive is narrower and more useful. If you're
picking a configuration to deploy on work in this difficulty band, Sol at
 low is the cheapest thing in this corpus that passes everything, and it
does it at roughly a 1.6x output-token advantage over Fable at medium 
(geometric mean across the 9 shared tasks). Whether Fable at some lower tier would
close that gap is a run I haven't done.

Finding 3: the effort knob never flipped a single outcome

Every model in this corpus exposes an "effort" knob (low/medium/high, or similar),
and the working assumption going in was that higher effort should mean better
outcomes. This is the one claim in the post where the corpus is unambiguous, because
it's a claim about matched pairs rather than an average.

§3 walks every adjacent pair of effort rungs, per model, matching runs by task
and repetition so task difficulty cancels out: Haiku 4.5 and its pinned snapshot,
Fable, Codex Spark, Luna, Kimi K3, and Sol's full five-rung ladder. That's 15
comparisons over 144 matched pairs. Across all of them, the number of discordant
pairs, meaning a task that passed at one effort tier and failed at the adjacent one,
is zero . Not "rarely," not "not statistically significant." Zero,
everywhere, for every model. The same holds for the two other paired contrasts in
the file: Fable against Sol at their best tiers (§2, 25 pairs) and bare against
harnessed invocation (§4, 27 pairs). Nothing in this corpus, turned in either
direction, ever moved a run across the pass/fail line.

What the knob did move is spend. Median output tokens per solved run, bare
invocation:

model low medium high xhigh max/ultra 

Sol 1,124 1,534 1,992 2,708 4,942 (ultra) 

GPT-5.6 Luna 1,551 2,874 5,249 (max) 

GPT-5.3 Codex Spark 2,308 3,530 4,250 

Kimi K3 1,384 1,630 1,972 (max) 

Fable 1,737 2,008 

Claude Haiku 4.5 2,860 2,674 2,745 (max) 

Claude Haiku 4.5 (pinned) 5,228 5,758 4,840 (max) 

Sol's ultra costs about 4.4x its low , and Luna's
 max about 3.4x its low , for zero additional passing runs.
Kimi climbs gently. Both Haiku rows are non-monotonic, and neither one has
 low as its cheapest tier, which is a good reminder that the knob's name
is a promise about intent and not a guarantee about behavior. (These medians are
descriptive, not a hypothesis test. They use the same output-tokens-only axis as
everything else here.)

The honest limit on this finding is the same ceiling effect from Finding 1. Effort
can't buy a pass on a task that already passes at the lowest tier. What this corpus
establishes is that on tasks in this difficulty band, the knob is pure cost. Whether
it earns its price on harder tasks is exactly the question the corpus can't answer
yet, and it's the strongest argument for making the task set harder before running
anything else.

Judged quality: two judges, checked against each other

Pass/fail is binary and, on this corpus, saturated. The judges are where the
finer-grained signal lives: correctness, simplicity, idiomatic style, and spec
adherence, each scored 0-10 by two separately-prompted judges (Claude and Codex)
that never see each other's output.

Before trusting either judge's score, I checked whether they agree. Averaging each
judge's four dimension scores into one per-run number and comparing those, the two
judges land within a point of each other on 95.7% of the 139 runs both judges
scored. Looking at the four dimensions individually instead of the per-run average,
agreement is tighter but still solid at 93.2% (518 of 556 judge-pairs within 1
point). Exact score matches are rarer (about 15% at the per-run level). The judges
converge on the same rough quality tier far more often than they converge on the
exact same integer, which is what I'd expect from two independently-prompted graders
and not a sign that one of them is noise.

With that agreement established, average judged scores (both judges, all four
dimensions) for the two models with enough judged runs to be worth reading:

model correctness simplicity idiomatic spec n 

Sol 9.33 9.06 8.93 9.55 80 

Fable 8.83 8.83 8.54 8.96 57 

Sol scores slightly higher across all four dimensions in this corpus, by about half
a point on a 0-10 scale. Put next to Finding 2, that's the only axis on which the
two models separate at all here: identical pass rates, no detectable cost difference
at matched tiers, and a small judged-quality edge to Sol. Half a point is also
inside the judges' own mean disagreement with each other (0.53 points, §7), so
I'd treat it as a hint about where to look next rather than a result. It's a smaller
and duller claim than "model X is better," and it's the one this data actually
carries.

One data-quality note, in the open

Not every run's token count came from a clean, direct measurement. Of 268 runs, 148
have tokens_in_status: measured (read directly off the CLI's own usage
reporting), 56 are recovered_in_ledger (reconstructed from a secondary
usage log after the primary read was incomplete), and 64 are
 quarantined , flagged as unreliable. The quarantine is not scattered
randomly: it's all 64 of Fable's rows, every one of them, while all 112 of Sol's are
measured. There is no trustworthy input-token number for Fable anywhere in this
corpus.

That's why every token figure in this post is output tokens only. It's a known rough
edge in how different CLIs report usage over long headless sessions, not a hidden
one, and the field exists specifically so a bad read fails loud in the data rather
than quietly averaging into a number that looks trustworthy. The next section is
what happens when you ignore it.

A correction I made to my own draft

The first version of this post led with a much better headline: same pass rate,
about a fifth of the tokens, p = 0.004. Sol used more tokens than Fable on all 9 of
9 matched tasks. It was a great chart. It was also wrong, and it was wrong in the
specific way this whole project exists to catch.

I had computed cost as tokens_in + tokens_out , which is the obvious
definition and the wrong one here, because Fable's tokens_in is
quarantined on 100% of its rows. I was comparing Fable's undercounted total against
Sol's complete one and reading the measurement gap as a performance gap. Worse, the
repo's own stats script had already been corrected for exactly this reason days
earlier, on 2026-07-30, and states the output-tokens-only rule in a comment. I
didn't run it. I recomputed the numbers by hand instead, and my hand-rolled version
quietly reintroduced the bug the script had been fixed to prevent.

Run the script and the flagship finding evaporates: p = 0.68, direction mixed,
nothing detectable. That's Finding 2 above.

I'm leaving this in the post rather than quietly fixing the numbers, for two
reasons. The first is that a benchmark asking you to trust its methodology should
show you the time its methodology caught the author. The second is that the failure
mode generalizes past me: a number that is 4.8x and p = 0.004 and confirms something
you already half-believed is exactly the number that doesn't get a second look. The
wrong chart is still in the repo under
 assets/model-eval-token-chart-WRONG-DO-NOT-USE.png , and it looks
completely convincing, which is the point.

Try it

No UI, no signup, no API key required for the smoke test:

git clone https://github.com/drakegriffith/model-eval
cd model-eval

# offline: proves the task is real by showing verify.sh
# fail, then pass, once the reference fix is applied
bash tasks/t1-py-a/selftest.sh

# exercises the full harness pipeline, no tokens spent,
# no API key needed
python3 runner/run.py --mock --limit 1

Point runner/run.py at your own Claude Code or Codex CLI (subscription
auth, no key needed) to run a live model against a task and see how it does.
 CONTRIBUTING.md covers adding a new task or a new model to the registry.

Repo: github.com/drakegriffith/model-eval

posts.title: I killed a week-long experiment because the thing I was testing had already read the answers
posts.excerpt: I spent about a week building a controlled experiment to find out whether my own setup is worth anything, and then I killed it. The setup is the pile of stuff I have bolted onto Claude Code over the last few months. A vault of notes, a stack of skills, a router file that tells th
posts.text:
I spent about a week building a controlled experiment to find out whether my own
setup is worth anything, and then I killed it. The setup is the pile of stuff I have
bolted onto Claude Code over the last few months. A vault of notes, a stack of
skills, a router file that tells the agent which skill to grab, a context layer, and
a memory system that carries what I learned in one repo into every other repo. It
all feels useful. Feels. Nobody had measured it, me least of all.

So: ablation study. Same tasks under the full stack, then again with one piece
pulled out at a time, and whatever hurts when you pull it is the piece doing work.
167 reps per cell. 8,183 runs. Pre-registered and frozen before a single run so I
could not drift the goalposts once numbers started landing, which I would have.

Zero of those runs happened.

The gate that ate it

Before a task's first scored run there is a check that greps every memory store on
the machine for that task's distinctive strings. If the answer is already sitting
somewhere an agent can retrieve, I am not measuring reasoning, I am measuring
lookup. Any hit burns the task. Fail-closed, no override switch, because the only
person who would ever reach for the override is me at 1am wanting the number.

All seven tasks burned. Nothing scored, ever.

The first cause is embarrassing and boring. I had sub-agents write the tasks on this
machine, so every task matched its own authoring transcript. Transcripts are memory.
I knew that. I had written it down in the same repo a week earlier, in a file about
this exact hazard. Moved the authoring off the machine, re-scanned, four of seven
came back clean.

Then the second cause.

The memory system had already filed it

My cross-project memory had consolidated pieces of the experiment into records
belonging to two unrelated projects. Spec revisions, task file paths, and in one case
the literal edit that introduced a task's answer string, sitting in a record filed
under a project that has nothing to do with any of this.

Nothing read the experiment's repo. There was no crawl to block, no directory to add
to an ignore list, no leak in the sense of something escaping through a hole. The
content showed up pre-formed, already summarized, filed while I worked. The memory
system was doing the job I built it for. The job is to notice what I am doing and
make it available later, in every other project. It did that. It is good at it.

And two of the conditions under test are memory and vault access. That is what kills
it. The leak is not even across arms. The full-stack arm can retrieve the leaked
answer, the stripped-down arm cannot reach it, so some slice of whatever gap I
measured is my own experiment handed back to me, and I would have read that slice as
the harness earning its keep. Which is the claim. That is the whole thing I sat down
to test.

If you run agent memory across projects and you also want to evaluate those agents on
anything, this is sitting there waiting for you. Your eval material is material. It
gets consolidated like everything else. The isolation you think you have is
repo-shaped, memory ignores repo shape, that is the product.

The bit I liked less

Writing up the kill I reread my own pre-registration and found something worse than
the leak, which is a sentence I did not enjoy typing.

Three tasks. One per task shape. 8,183 runs across three tasks. All that repetition
buys precision and precision is not generality, so I would have finished with a very
tight measurement of three specific tasks and no standing to say a word about a
fourth. The limitation is written into the pre-registration. In my own words. I read
it during review and approved it, because the run count looked serious and I wanted
to start.

So the clean version of this experiment was going to hand me a number I could not
use. I got saved from that by a grep.

What I am doing instead

Bake-off on real tickets out of live repos. Full stack against bare, same ticket,
judged blind. Contamination stops mattering once the tasks are work I wanted done
anyway, and if the harness wins partly by retrieving something it stashed earlier,
fine, that is the harness doing its job. Looser instrument. Worse paper. Measures a
thing I care about.

The actual mistake was sequencing. I built the apparatus first, all of it,
pre-registration and frozen spec and an adversarial review panel and contamination
scanning and isolation proofs, and the apparatus is good. I built it before checking
whether the thing I wanted to measure was measurable on this machine, with this
memory running, on tasks of this kind. That check is an afternoon. It goes first, and
I knew that, and I did it in the other order anyway.

posts.title: I asked two AI models to destroy my work. They disagreed about how.
posts.excerpt: For the last few weeks I have been designing a piece of software, and before any decision gets locked I hand the write-up to two AI models and ask them to break it. Kimi and Codex. Same brief, sent in parallel. Neither can see the other's response, and neither remembers the last
posts.text:
For the last few weeks I have been designing a piece of software, and before any
decision gets locked I hand the write-up to two AI models and ask them to break
it. Kimi and Codex. Same brief, sent in parallel. Neither can see the other's
response, and neither remembers the last round.

The setup was meant to catch my mistakes, which it does. It also taught me
something about reviewing that I did not go looking for.

Same brief, different reviewers

The important detail first, because it is what makes the rest meaningful: both
models get the identical file. Same bytes. Same opening line telling them they
are an adversarial reviewer and should default to skepticism. Neither one is
told to be harsher than the other.

Here is what came back on the same document, on the same day.

Kimi 
 Codex 

words 
 2,706 
 1,915 

numeric claims 
 15 
 6 

bullet points 
 31 
 88 

average sentence length 
 31.8 words 
 31.9 words 

Average sentence length matches to a tenth of a word, so neither is padding.
What differs is where they go.

Kimi is the empiricist. It re-ran my measurement script, without being asked to,
and compared its own output against the figures I had published. That is how it
found the error: I had been counting text written by AI subagents as though a
human had typed it. I published 10.6 percent as 14.4 percent. It then quoted my
own script's documentation back at me, which had warned against exactly that
mistake. I had written the warning and then ignored it.

Codex is the structuralist. It went looking for my experiments folder before
reading anything, and attacked the shape of my argument rather than its
arithmetic. Its finding was that my headline metric multiplied five rates
measured over four different populations. The arithmetic was correct. The number
meant nothing.

Then both of them opened with the same two objections. They run in parallel,
memoryless, unable to coordinate. That agreement carried more weight than either
review alone, and it convinced me to rebuild the document rather than patch it.

The two days I spent trying to make one of them fair

Kimi has a habit that took me a while to understand. It never stops. Every round
produces fresh criticism, all of it individually defensible, and I could keep
revising forever without ever arriving at "this is finished."

For a while I read that as temperament, so I tried to fix it the way everyone
tries to fix it. I rewrote the instructions.

I ran this properly, over three days in July, with a sealed holdout set and a
pre-registered decision rule. The question was narrow: can any wording make this
model a useful pass-or-fail gate on a specification? I gave it more context, then
less. I told it to be harsher. I told it to be gentler. I moved the stated
failure rate up and down, and the stated cost of missing something.

The answer was no, and the shape of the no is the part worth having.

It flagged 82 percent of specifications when 35 percent of them were actually
bad. A rubber stamp that read nothing and approved everything scored better than
every prompt I wrote. On obviously good specs and obviously terrible ones it was
perfect. On real ones it was a coin flip.

Every tone lever moved the flag rate and none of them improved the accuracy.
Tilting it toward flagging produced nine false alarms and zero real catches. Its
sense of what looks risky turns out to be uncorrelated with what is actually
broken. This is the finding I keep coming back to, because "just tell it to be
more critical" is the first thing anyone reaches for and it is worse than
useless. It produces more noise that feels like more rigour.

More instruction made it monotonically worse. Every added distinction raised its
flagging without adding a single new catch. One rewrite collapsed it into
approving everything.

My best configuration scored 44 out of 50 on the data I tuned it against, then
caught zero of three real failures on the sealed holdout. It had memorised the
phrasing of the examples I let it see rather than learning anything.

I filed the whole thing as a failed experiment and moved on.

It was not a failed experiment

Three days later I was writing up the review process and realised the null result
was the load-bearing part.

The model that loses to a rubber stamp on pass-or-fail is the same model that
re-ran my script and caught a real error in my published numbers. Both of those
are true at once, and I had been treating them as one purchase.

Finding things and judging things are separate skills, and this reviewer has one
of them.

So the process I ended up with never asks a model for a verdict. It asks for
findings, and every finding has to cite a line, a number, or a specific
inference. Anything that cannot point at something is advisory by default.
Findings get sorted into fatal, material, and advisory, and only fatal blocks
acceptance.

Review stops when a round produces nothing fatal, with a hard cap of three
rounds. And the rule that actually made it terminate: later rounds may only check
whether earlier findings were resolved. They may not open new ground. New ground
becomes a separate task.

Without that last rule, every round legitimately discovers something new, because
any document is infinitely criticisable, and the sequence never ends. With it,
the loop is bounded by the first round's findings, which is a finite list. The
reviewer stopped being the thing that decides when I am done, which was the real
problem all along. Before, that decision was made by whatever hour I ran out of
patience.

A postscript about losing my own work

While writing this I could not find the three-day experiment I just described. It
was on my own laptop, committed to git, in a folder two directories from where I
was working, finished the previous week.

I searched for "prompt engineering." I searched for "tone" across 3,483
conversation transcripts. I ran a full content search across every project folder
for "harsh," "be kind," and half a dozen similar phrases. All of it came back
empty, or came back with results about email etiquette.

The document that answered the question was sitting right there. It just never
uses those words. It says propensity levers, base rate, cost asymmetry, flag
rate. I had named the work for what it measured, and I went looking for it using
the words I would have described it with months later. Both descriptions are
correct. They share no vocabulary.

What eventually found it was listing my folders by date and reading the names.

Nothing was lost, corrupted, or missing. Storage was perfect. Retrieval failed
completely, on the gap between how I filed something and how I later asked for
it. That is a more honest argument for better search than any benchmark I could
have designed, and I got it by accident, from failing at it.

Two caveats, because they matter

The prompt was identical for both models. The surrounding software was not: each
runs through its own command line tool with its own defaults. The comparison is
controlled on instructions and imperfectly controlled on environment, and a
cleaner version of this would hold both fixed.

The calibration result is about one model at one task, gating specifications. It
is not a claim about that model generally, and it is certainly not a claim about
the others. What generalises is the method: measure your reviewer against a
baseline that does nothing before you trust its verdicts, because a reviewer that
flags most things can look rigorous while carrying no information at all.
